t: You just picked up a cup.
Crack. Now there's a handle in your hand. And the cup is on the floor.
Yesterday you won a fight in a minute. Today you lost to the dishes.
Mom, do we have any metal cups?
That's the small stuff. One day something alive will land in that hand. Lighter than a cup.
What if you became Mike Tyson? You'd get his punch, his speed, and his road.
Let's rewind a little.
Your name is Danya, you're fifteen. The strongest thing you've done with your hands is open a jar of pickles. On the third try.
On your building's roof there's a pigeon loft. Forty birds, and you know each by sight.
Back to your chickens again?
They're racing pigeons. They're smarter than you.
Lyokha is your friend. He has a theory for everything and proof for nothing.
And then an ordinary morning comes. You reach to turn off the alarm clock.
And the alarm clock goes into the nightstand. Up to its hands.
I... just pressed it.
You walk to the door. Take the handle. Crack.
In the yard, Gera from the third entrance is waiting. Two years he's collected your change. On schedule.
He swings, just for show. And suddenly you're below his fist. And off to the side.
Your hand answers on its own. Gera flies onto the bench. Sits up straight, like in an armchair. And gets up offended.
Sorry! I didn't mean to!
The whole yard is looking at you. You're looking at your fist. And it clenches.
Tyson's story began in Brownsville, Brooklyn. By his own account, he kept pigeons as a kid.
You have pigeons too. Only now it's scary to go near them.
Right. We need a scientific approach.
Experiment one. A pencil. You pick it up the way people pick up a pencil.
Splinters.
Interesting. Now a glass.
Experiment two. You try very hard. Gently. Two fingers.
The glass holds for a whole second.
Experiment three. An egg.
You figured out everything about the egg from the umbrella.
Conclusion. You've become too strong for things.
Rule number one: the stronger you are, the more fragile the world around you.
Sounds logical. Remember that rule.
So what now, I shouldn't touch anything?
Or find someone who touches things the right way.
In nineteen eighty-four, scientists Westling and Johansson measured how people hold things.
It turned out we squeeze an object a little harder than needed so it won't slip. Just a little.
Your margin is now like a hydraulic press.
A basement gym. It smells of leather and chlorine. The coach is Semyon Ilyich, and he won't shake your hand.
Saw what you did to your door handle. Come in.
Tyson had a coach, Cus D'Amato. They met when Mike was about thirteen.
D'Amato taught the peek-a-boo style: hands at your face, body swaying, punches by number.
Seven! Two! Three!
You learn the numbers in a day. The slips in two. The body knows it all itself.
On day three you take a light slap from the mitt. Then another.
Semyon Ilyich lowers the mitts and looks for a long time. Not at your hands. At your shoulders. They're up by your ears.
Shoulders down. You're not carrying a wardrobe.
You lower your shoulders. For four seconds. Then they creep back up.
The coach writes something in a notebook and underlines it twice.
And then Semyon Ilyich takes out an egg.
Hit it. And stop a centimeter short.
The first egg. You aim and clench your fist till it creaks.
The second. The third. The coach silently wipes the ring.
Exhale. Watch the egg, not your hand.
You exhale. You watch the egg. The fist flies, and stops. A centimeter away.
Now catch.
Your palm goes down with the egg. Like a hammock. The egg lies in your hand. Whole.
How did I do that?!
When you figure it out, come back for the belt.
You didn't figure it out. You decided you were just lucky.
Your first fight. A community hall, two hundred spectators. Your opponent is older, heavier, and sure you used the wrong door.
Gong. Slip. Seven, two, three. The referee counts to ten, and you look at the clock. A minute has passed.
And the next morning you simply pick up a cup.
Crack. A handle in your hand. The cup on the floor. Yesterday you won a fight in a minute. Today you lost to the dishes.
Mom, do we have any metal cups?
We do. It's called a saucepan.
Tyson's first nineteen professional fights ended in knockouts. Twelve in the first round.
Yours come out the same. Fight, knockout. Home, a phone.
Fight, knockout. Home, a key stays in the lock. Separate from the head.
Fight, knockout. Home, a spoon. The third one this week.
You eat with a plastic fork and carry bags on your elbows. Like a penguin.
And once, something strange happens. You and Lyokha are arguing on the roof.
Speaking of penguins. Penguins are fish!
They have feathers, Lyokha. Feathers!
You argue for four minutes. The whole time you're holding a glass bottle. Whole.
Then you notice it.
Clink.
Note to self: penguins break bottles.
Before the big fight Semyon Ilyich doesn't come to the gym.
You're left with the bag, the numbers, and hands nobody tells to "exhale" anymore.
Tyson had it harder. Cus D'Amato died on the fourth of November, nineteen eighty-five. A year before his student's biggest fight.
You hang the coach's cap on a nail. Next to the door handle. Very carefully. The nail bends.
On the twenty-second of November, nineteen eighty-six, Tyson won the title in the second round.
He was twenty years, four months and twenty-two days old. No heavyweight champion had been younger.
You're twenty too. Ten thousand in the arena. The second round. Seven, two, three.
They put the belt on you. Heavy, golden. You squeeze your eyes shut and wait for the crack.
No crack. You're not holding the belt. It just rests on your shoulder.
At home, everything is as it was. Mom's glasses.
The frame with your photo together.
The tap. The light switch. The TV remote.
Danechka. My champion. Come here.
Mom hugs you. You stand with your arms at your sides, fists clenched, counting seconds until she lets go.
Why are you so stiff, like wood?
Tired, Mom.
Then, fast. In eighty-seven Tyson held three belts. In eighty-eight he put Michael Spinks down in ninety-one seconds.
Now you have three belts too, a big house, and people who open doors for you. Literally.
The handles in the house are steel. The cups are rubber. They still changed the steering wheel twice.
The railings. The bathroom tap. The lid of a piano nobody plays.
You moved the pigeon loft to the new roof. You scatter grain from a shovel. From three steps away.
In a nest at the edge there's a chick. Three weeks old, and the loudest peeper.
You used to take chicks like this into your palms and warm them. You reach out. Almost touching the down.
And you pull back. Your hand finds the parapet. The parapet cracks.
The chick looks at you and peeps. You feed it from the shovel.
I've got a theory. An egg. On my command.
Relax! Relax harder!
You relax with all your strength.
Turns out you can't relax with all your strength.
Note to self: on command doesn't work.
In a week, Tokyo. An opponent almost nobody bets on. Forty-two to one, in your favor.
I'll take him with my left hand.
The eleventh of February, nineteen ninety, Tokyo. Tyson has thirty-seven wins and no losses.
In round ten James Douglas knocked him out. The same forty-two to one.
Your Tokyo looks like this. You step into the ring and don't warm up. Why bother.
Round one. You swing with everything you've got. And miss.
Round three. The opponent punches softly. But often. Every time he lands where you stand. You keep standing.
Round five. You hit even harder. Shoulders like stone, neck like a post. The slips ended three rounds ago.
Seven, two... The third number doesn't come. Your fist is clenched so hard it can't make it in time.
Round ten. You see a glove. Then the ceiling. Then the referee, who is now counting for you.
You get up when it's all over. You grab the rope. The rope snaps.
The locker room. A plane. Home. You break everything you touch. And for once you don't even notice.
Night. You're on the roof. Sitting on your own hands so you won't touch anything.
Where are you? I'm bringing tea. In a saucepan.
A peep. The chick has climbed out and is walking along the ledge. Below it, five floors and tile.
Option one. Put a box under it.
Option two. A net. The handle snaps in half.
Option three. Touch nothing and wait for Lyokha. Lyokha is on the third floor.
The chick takes another step. Its foot slips.
Relax. Relax. Come on, relax already!
It doesn't work. You've been here before. The harder you order your hand, the tighter it clenches.
And then you remember the bottle.
You held it four minutes and didn't break it. Because you weren't looking at your hand. You were looking at Lyokha.
And now everything else. The cup. The handle. The pencil. The key. The glasses. You watch your hand. Knuckles white.
"Watch the egg, not your hand."
Lyokha! Talk! Anything!
Uh... Penguins are fish after all!
They have feathers!
The chick falls.
You look only at it. Exhale. Your palm goes down with it. Like a hammock.
Silence.
It's sitting in your palm. Warm. Angry. Alive.
You don't remember opening your fingers.
Did I miss everything?
Lyokha pours tea. Without thinking, you take the cup from him. An ordinary porcelain one.
The cup is whole.
Rule number one was wrong. The world didn't become fragile because you became strong.
Things broke when you clenched. When you were afraid to break them. When you held on to control with both hands.
In twenty ten, McGill and colleagues recorded the muscles of five strong fighters. Their punches came in two peaks.
Tense, release, tense. By their conclusion, the arm speeds up between the peaks.
In Tokyo you didn't lose because you got weaker. You hit with everything, and speed is born where muscles let go.
In the morning you go down to the basement. Semyon Ilyich is back. You bring him one egg.
No belt. Why did you come?
Got it. Throw it.
He throws. You watch the egg. Exhale. Palm. Whole.
He opens the notebook. There's one word. Underlined twice.
Well, there. Now we can talk about the belt.
In the evening you come home. And Mom, as always, goes to hug you.
You hug her first. With both arms. Nothing cracks.
Finally. Not like wood.
The strength stayed with you. All of it. Only the fear left.
What are you afraid to break, if you're strong?
